title: Numbers One to Ten
title_arabic: من واحد لين عشرة — بكم هذا؟
description: Count to ten, ask how much something costs, understand the answer, and read a phone number digit by digit — the Gulf way, with the short forms people actually say in front of nouns.
approach: Counting with fingers on screen, then prices: every number is heard alone, then in a price, then in a phone number. Production from the first minute — numbers are the safest words to say aloud.
unlock_condition: ≥10/12 on the hear-the-price quiz and a recorded count from one to ten
can_do: Ask how much something costs and understand the answer
Say a phone number digit by digit

grammar.title: بكم؟ and كم؟ — how much, how many
grammar.explanation: For a price you ask بكم؟ — literally 'with how much' — and put the thing before or after: بكم هذا؟, بكم القهوة؟. The answer comes back with the same بـ: بخمسة ريال (for five riyals). To ask how many of something, use كم with the thing in the singular: كم ولد؟ how many boys. You will hear Kuwaitis say بچم with a ch — same word. Neither question needs any extra grammar: the question word and the noun are the whole sentence.

examples.english: How much is the tea? — Two riyals
How many boys do you have? — Three

culture.title: Riyal, dirham, dinar — and the small change
culture.note: Saudi Arabia and Qatar count in ريال, the Emirates in درهم, Kuwait and Bahrain in دينار — and a Kuwaiti dinar is worth about twelve Saudi riyals, so the numbers you hear in a Kuwaiti vlog are much smaller. Small change is هللة in Saudi and فلس in Kuwait, Bahrain and the Emirates. Cards and phone payment are everywhere now, but a corner shop (بقالة) still expects you to know the price as a spoken number, and a taxi driver will say it once, fast.

culture.title: The first price is rarely the last
culture.note: In a traditional souq — المباركية in Kuwait, سوق واقف in Doha, البلد in Jeddah — a first price is an opening. The polite move is not to argue but to say غالي (expensive) with a smile and ask for a little off: رخّص شوي. In a mall or supermarket the price on the tag is the price, and bargaining would be strange. Either way, thank the seller with يعطيك العافية as you leave.

phrases.english: Bring it down a little, please

vocabulary.teaching_note: The only number that comes after the noun: بيت واحد (one house), بنت وحدة (one girl — the feminine is وحدة waḥda). On its own it also means 'someone': فيه واحد بالباب.
vocabulary.image_scene: A single hand holding up one finger, one date on a plate beside it.
vocabulary.video_hint: Ordering one of something; counting on fingers; children's counting songs.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Said thnayn, without the MSA initial i. Feminine ثنتين thintayn. With a noun, Gulf uses the dual ending -ayn instead: بيتين two houses, ريالين two riyals, قهوتين two coffees. Also the name of Monday (الاثنين).
vocabulary.image_scene: A hand holding up two fingers, two small coffee cups on a tray beside it.
vocabulary.video_hint: Ordering two of something; the -ayn dual on nouns in prices.

vocabulary.teaching_note: From three to ten Gulf speakers use the short form before a noun — ثلاث كتب, ثلاث بنات — and the long form ثلاثة when counting or saying a price on its own. Do not drill the MSA gender-flip; Gulf speech is relaxed about it.
vocabulary.image_scene: A hand holding up three fingers, three books stacked beside it.
vocabulary.video_hint: Counting items in a challenge; prices of three riyals/dirhams.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Ends in ع — the squeezed throat sound — as do seven, nine and ten. Long form أربعة arbaʿa. Also in الأربعا, Wednesday.
vocabulary.image_scene: A hand holding up four fingers, four chairs around a small table beside it.
vocabulary.video_hint: Counting seats or people; prices of four.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Starts with the rasping خ from خبز. Long form خمسة khamsa — the number you will hear most in prices, because five riyals and five dirhams buy a lot of small things.
vocabulary.image_scene: An open hand showing five fingers, a five-riyal banknote beside it.
vocabulary.video_hint: A vendor saying خمسة; the five-note in a shopping vlog.

vocabulary.teaching_note: A doubled t: sitt. Long form ستة sitta. Do not confuse with the Egyptian ست (lady) — in the Gulf a lady is حرمة.
vocabulary.image_scene: Six eggs in a carton, a hand showing five fingers plus one beside it.
vocabulary.video_hint: Counting eggs or items in a cooking clip; prices of six.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Ends in ع again. Long form سبعة sabʿa. Before a word starting with a vowel you may hear سبعت — سبعت أيام, seven days.
vocabulary.image_scene: A hand and two fingers of another hand making seven, seven dates in a row.
vocabulary.video_hint: Days of a trip counted; seven riyals/dirhams.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The odd one: the short form ends in n, the long form ثمانية thimaanya. Starts with ث, the 'think' sound the Gulf keeps.
vocabulary.image_scene: Eight small tea glasses on a round tray.
vocabulary.video_hint: Working hours or a time of day; prices of eight.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Short i, final ع. Long form تسعة tisʿa. Keep it apart from سبع (seven): tisʿ starts with t, sabʿ with s.
vocabulary.image_scene: Nine oranges arranged in a three-by-three square.
vocabulary.video_hint: Phone numbers read out; prices of nine.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Said ʿashar with a helping vowel; long form عشرة ʿashra. Both start with ع. The ten-note is the everyday banknote across the Gulf, so عشرة is the price you will hear second-most after five.
vocabulary.image_scene: Two open hands showing ten fingers, a ten-riyal note between them.
vocabulary.video_hint: A vendor saying عشرة; the ten-note changing hands.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The price question, everywhere in the Gulf. Kuwaitis say بچم bicham. Add the thing: بكم هذا؟, بكم القهوة؟. The answer repeats the بـ: بعشرة.
vocabulary.image_scene: A shopper holding up a small item toward a stallholder with a questioning face.
vocabulary.video_hint: Souq and market vlogs; price challenges; the moment before a vendor answers.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The plural of فلس (a small coin) is the ordinary word for money in every Gulf country — never نقود. Emiratis also say بيزات. Watch the long uu.
vocabulary.image_scene: A hand holding a fan of Gulf banknotes of different colours.

example.english: Do you have money on you?

vocabulary.video_hint: Budget challenges; someone checking a wallet.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Learn the currency of the country you are aiming at: ريال in Saudi Arabia and Qatar, درهم dirham in the Emirates, دينار diinaar in Kuwait and Bahrain. After a number the singular is used: خمسة ريال, عشرة درهم.
vocabulary.image_scene: A Saudi banknote and a few coins on a shop counter.
vocabulary.video_hint: Prices quoted in a shop; banknotes on screen.

dialogue.speaker: Sara
dialogue.arabic: خمسة خمسة ثنين — أربعة ثلاثة سبعة واحد
dialogue.transliteration: khamsa khamsa thnayn — arbaʿa thalaatha sabʿa waaḥid
dialogue.english: Five five two — four three seven one

sound_spotlight.explanation: Three of the ten numbers start with the 'think' sound. Gulf keeps it where Cairo says s or t, so if you hear talaata the speaker is not from the Gulf. Practise with the tip of the tongue between the teeth.

sound_spotlight.example: أربع، سبع، تسع، عشر (arbaʿ, sabʿ, tisʿ, ʿashar)
sound_spotlight.explanation: Four numbers carry ع — the throat squeeze. At the end of a word it sounds like a short catch that colours the vowel before it. Say the number, then close the throat for a moment.
Numbers travel with the things you buy, and the things you buy keep the Gulf hard g: gahwa, suug. Hearing g here confirms you are in the right dialect.

lesson_sequence.detail: A souq stall with dates and small change. One line of English: today you count and ask the price. Tap يلّا.
Ten cards, fingers on screen; audio plays the short form then the long form. Learner repeats each into the mic; the counter climbs.
A price plays (بخمسة ريال); the learner taps the right banknote or number. Twelve items across 1–10 with riyal, dirham and dinar.
Six objects from Lesson 1 appear; the learner records بكم + the object; a native answers with a price; the learner taps what they heard.
A number is read digit by digit; the learner types it. Then the learner records their own number and hears it played back by a native voice.
The souq dialogue plays; then twelve audio-only items mixing numbers, prices and بكم.
Counter rolls to 78. Nudge: read the price of the next three things you buy out loud, in Arabic.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Count the chairs, cups or people in the room right now: واحد، ثنين، ثلاث…
real_world_prompts.context: Lesson-complete screen. Here-and-now counting with no partner needed.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Say your own phone number in Arabic, digit by digit, three times today.
real_world_prompts.context: Next-day notification. The one number every learner needs to produce under pressure.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Ask your tutor to play shopkeeper: you ask بكم هذا؟ for five objects and repeat each price back.
real_world_prompts.context: Before a tutor session. Question plus comprehension loop.
